title: The Fish That Live Where Sunlight Dies

sentences.t: Two hundred meters below the surface of the ocean, the sunlight starts to give up.
By a thousand meters, it's gone completely, and in between is a place scientists call the twilight zone.
It's dim, it's cold, and it might hold more fish, by weight, than every other part of the ocean put together.
And almost nobody has heard of the animals that live there.
Take the bristlemouth, a little fish about the size of your finger.
There are so many bristlemouths that it's probably the most common vertebrate on the entire planet.
More common than chickens, more common than rats, more common than us.
And yet, until fairly recently, we barely knew they existed, because they live in a place we almost never go.
So how do you survive somewhere that dark?
The first trick is light itself.
Around three quarters of the animals in the twilight zone can make their own light, a process called bioluminescence.
Some use it to find a mate, some use it to lure in dinner, and some use it to vanish.

Okay, back to vanishing.
Many twilight zone fish have rows of tiny lights along their bellies, called photophores.
From below, a predator looks up and sees a silhouette against the faint light from above.
So these fish match that light exactly, brightness and colour, and their silhouette basically disappears.
It's called counter-illumination, and it's one of the cleverest pieces of camouflage in nature.
The second trick is moving, and moving a lot.
Every night, as the sun sets, billions of these animals swim up toward the surface to feed in the dark, and then swim back down before dawn.
It's called the diel vertical migration, and it's the largest migration on Earth, happening every single night.
For a fish the size of a finger, that can mean swimming several hundred meters up and back, every day.
That's like you jogging a marathon before breakfast, and then another one before bed.
And this daily trip matters to all of us, not just the fish.
When they feed near the surface and swim back down, they carry carbon with them, into the deep ocean.
Some researchers think this is a big part of how the ocean pulls carbon out of the air.
Which is why it's worrying that there's growing interest in fishing the twilight zone for fishmeal and supplements.
We don't yet know how much we can take before we break something we don't understand.
